lessons.title: If: -(으)면
lessons.learn: The all-round IF! 먹으면 (if I eat), 가면 (if I go), 비가 오면 (if it rains). Vowel-stems: -면, consonants: -으면! 와도 (even if): 와도 가요 = Even if it rains, I go!

grammar.title: -(으)면 (if) · -아/어도 (even if)
grammar.explain: 먹으면 (if eat), 가면 (if go). 비가 오면 안 가요 (if it rains, I won't go). 와도 가요 (even if rains, go)! 공부하면 알아요 (if you study, you know)!

examples.en: If it rains, I won't go.
If you study, you know.
Even if it rains, I'll go!

dialogue.en: If it rains tomorrow, what will you do?
Even if it rains, I'll go!

lessons.title: Let's and decisions: ㅂ시다/기로
lessons.learn: Formal LET'S! 갑시다 (let's go), 먹읍시다 (let's eat), 합시다! Decide: -기로 했어요 (I decided to): 가기로 했어요! Plans set: 예정이에요. Rally the group!

grammar.title: -(으)ㅂ시다 + -기로 했어요
grammar.explain: 갑시다! (let's go!), 먹읍시다! Plans decided: 한국에 가기로 했어요 (I decided to go to Korea). 예정: 갈 예정이에요 (scheduled to go)!

examples.en: Let's eat together!
I decided to go to Korea.

lessons.title: 계획이 바뀔 때
lessons.learn: A plan that did not happen is told with -(으)려고 했어요, and what replaced it is named with 대신에. When nothing could have been done the phrase is 어쩔 수 없이, which takes the whole sentence and never a second verb.

grammar.title: Intentions that changed
grammar.pattern: 가려고 했어요 · 비가 와서 못 갔어요 · 그 대신에 집에서 일했어요
grammar.explain: -(으)려고 했어요 states what you intended before the change, and the outcome needs its own predicate: 비가 와서 못 갔어요. 대신에 then names the replacement inside one clause — 영화 대신에 커피, not two 대신에 in a row.

examples.en: I was going to go hiking at the weekend.
It rained, so I could not go.
Instead of hiking I watched a film at home.

mistakes.why: -(으)려고 했어요 already carries the intention; the action is not added after it.

mistakes.wrong: 대신에 영화를 봤어요 대신에 커피를 마셨어요.
mistakes.why: 대신에 replaces one noun with another inside a single clause.

dialogue.t: 아니요, 등산 대신에 집에서 보고서를 썼어요.
dialogue.r: aniyo, deungsan daesin-e jib-eseo bogoseo-reul sseosseoyo.
dialogue.en: No — instead of hiking I wrote a report at home.

lessons.title: Full honorifics: -시-
lessons.learn: Honor in every verb! -시- infix: 가세요 (honorific go), 드세요 (honorific eat), 주무세요 (honorific sleep), 계세요 (honorific be). Honorific nouns: 말씀 (words), 성함 (name), 댁 (home)!

grammar.title: -시- infix + honorific nouns
grammar.explain: 선생님이 계세요? (Is the teacher there?). 잡수세요 = honorific eat (alt). 말씀하세요 (please speak, honored). Humble ME: 드리다 (I humbly give)!
grammar.pattern: -시- for elders · humble 드리다/저 for self

examples.en: Is the teacher there? (honorific)
Eat a lot! (honorific)
I'll do it for you. (humble)

mistakes: Using -시- for YOURSELF — honorifics elevate OTHERS!
Saying 이름 to elders — their name: 성함!

lessons.title: Debate connectors
lessons.learn: Argue elegantly! 하지만 (but/however), 그래서 (so), 즉 (in other words), 예를 들어 (for example), 게다가 (besides), 결국 (after all). Chain: 예를 들어…게다가…그래서…!

grammar.title: Connector chains
grammar.explain: 지하철은 편리해요. 하지만 복잡해요. 즉, 좋아요! (The subway is handy. But crowded. In short, good!). Start sentences with 하지만/그래서/즉!

examples.en: The subway is handy. However, it's crowded.
For example, Seoul is big.
In short, the subway is good!

mistakes: Saying 하지만 at sentence END — 하지만 starts sentences!

lessons.learn: Disagreement at work accepts the point it can accept, then objects: -기는 하지만 carries the concession and 우려가 있습니다 adds the objection without closing the door.

grammar.title: Conceding before objecting
grammar.pattern: 그 점은 이해하지만 · 효과가 있기는 하지만 · 다른 관점에서 보면
grammar.explain: -기는 하지만 acknowledges the strength of the other position before the objection, which is why it needs a real contrast after it. 다른 관점에서 보면 shifts the frame instead of attacking the person, and 우려가 있습니다 states the objection as a risk.

examples.en: I understand that point, but cost is the problem.
It is true that there is an effect, but it is not enough.

examples.t: 다른 관점에서 보면 위험이 더 큽니다.
examples.r: dareun gwanjeom-eseo bomyeon wiheom-i deo keumnida.
examples.en: From another point of view the risk is larger.

mistakes.right: 그 점은 이해하지만 다른 문제가 있습니다.
mistakes.why: In a Korean meeting the conceded point is named first; a flat 틀렸습니다 closes the room.
-기는 하지만 demands a genuine contrast after it.

dialogue.r: dareun gwanjeom-eseo bomyeon illyeok-i du bae piryohamnida.

lessons.title: Korean culture: 정 and food
lessons.learn: Culture time! 정 (deep affection/bond), 김치, 비빔밥, 한복 (traditional dress), 추석 (harvest festival). Have-tried: -아/어 봤어요: 김치를 먹어 봤어요? Guests first — 손님은 왕!

grammar.title: -아/어 봤어요: have tried
grammar.explain: 김치를 먹어 봤어요? (Have you tried kimchi?), 한복을 입어 봤어요 (I've tried hanbok)! 아/어 + 봤어요 = try-experience!

examples.en: Have you tried kimchi?
I've tried bibimbap!
I've been to Korea. (tried going)

mistakes: Saying 먹은 봤어요 — try needs 아/어: 먹어 봤어요!
Saying 봤어요 for simple past — 봤어요 = tried/seen!

lessons.title: Storytelling: 옛날 옛적에
lessons.learn: Graduation! 옛날 옛적에 (long ago), 어느 날 (one day), 갑자기 (suddenly), 마침내 (at last), 마지막으로 (finally). Mix tenses: 갔어요, 먹고 있었어요, 먹고 싶어요! Tell YOUR Seoul story!

grammar.title: Story spine: 옛날 옛적에…마지막으로
grammar.explain: 옛날 옛적에…어느 날…갑자기…마침내…마지막으로 — the five-beat Korean story spine. Add 봤어요, 면, honorifics — graduate in style!
grammar.pattern: 옛날 옛적에 → 어느 날 → 갑자기 → 마지막으로

examples.en: Long ago, I went to Seoul.
Suddenly, it snowed!
Finally, I returned home.

mistakes: Starting tales with 어제 — stories open 옛날 옛적에!
Staying in 요-past only — mix 있었어요 + 싶어요!

lessons.title: 속담으로 조언하기
lessons.learn: A proverb enters a sentence as a quotation: 속담에 …라는 말이 있어요. The metaphor itself is the predicate, so it takes no second noun, and the advice is finished with -는 게 좋겠어요.

grammar.title: Quoting a proverb
grammar.pattern: 속담에 티끌 모아 태산이라는 말이 있어요 · 그는 우물 안 개구리예요
grammar.explain: A proverb is introduced with -라는 말이 있다. When it is applied to a person the metaphor stands as the predicate by itself: 그는 우물 안 개구리예요, with no 사람 or other noun added.

examples.t: 속담에 티끌 모아 태산이라는 말이 있어요.
examples.r: sokdam-e tikkeul moa taesan-iraneun mal-i isseoyo.
examples.en: There is a proverb: gather the dust and it becomes a mountain.
If you save a little at a time it becomes a lot.
He is a frog in a well.

mistakes.why: A proverb is quoted with -라는 말이 있다, not owned by 있다.
The metaphor is the whole predicate; a second noun cannot follow it.

dialogue.t: 지훈 씨는 왜 매일 조금씩 저축해요?
dialogue.r: jihun ssi-neun wae maeil jogeumssik jeochukhaeyo?
dialogue.en: Jihun, why do you save a little every day?

dialogue.t: 속담에 티끌 모아 태산이라는 말이 있잖아요.
dialogue.r: sokdam-e tikkeul moa taesan-iraneun mal-i itjanayo.
dialogue.en: You know the proverb: gather the dust and it becomes a mountain.

dialogue.t: 그 말은 맞지만 요즘은 물가가 올라요.
dialogue.r: geu mal-eun matjiman yojeum-eun mulga-ga ollayo.
dialogue.en: That is true, but prices are rising these days.

dialogue.t: 그래도 안 모으면 더 힘들어요. 조금씩 모으는 게 좋겠어요.
dialogue.r: geuraedo an moeumyeon deo himdeureoyo. jogeumssik moeuneun ge jotgesseoyo.
dialogue.en: Even so, it is harder if you save nothing. Better to save a little at a time.

culture.text: 정 is the Korean word for the bond that accumulates between people who have shared time, food and difficulty. It cannot be bought or hurried, and the language treats it as something you 감정을 쌓다, pile up. It explains a great deal of Korean professional life: a team will eat together after work, and a favour refused outright is rarer than a favour accepted slowly. In a debate, the same 정 means disagreement is usually wrapped in a frame that keeps the relationship intact.

reading.text: 토론에서 이기는 것보다 중요한 것은 상대의 주장을 정확히 이해하는 일입니다. 상대가 근거를 제시하면 먼저 인정하고, 그다음에 제 한계를 지적해야 합니다. 그러나 감정적인 표현은 설득력을 떨어뜨립니다. 예를 들어 우리가 이 자료를 믿을 수 있다면 결론도 받아들일 수 있습니다. 반대로 근거가 약하면 결론을 보류하는 것이 옳습니다. 좋은 토론은 이기고 지는 것이 아니라 함께 더 나은 결정에 이르는 과정입니다.
reading.gloss: In a debate, understanding the other side's argument exactly matters more than winning. When they offer evidence, acknowledge it first and only then point out its limits. Emotional phrasing, however, weakens persuasion. For example, if we can trust this data we can also accept the conclusion. If the evidence is weak, on the other hand, the right move is to hold the conclusion back. A good debate is not winning and losing but a process of arriving at a better decision together.

동료: 그럼 결정을 취소해야 한다고 보십니까?
분석자: 아니요, 조건을 붙여서 유지하는 편이 낫습니다.

listening.gloss: Colleague: Was this decision not too fast? Analyst: Speed is not the problem. Weak evidence is the problem. Colleague: Then do you think the decision should be cancelled? Analyst: No — it is better to keep it with conditions attached. Colleague: For example, what conditions?

mistakes.why: 뵙다 inserts ㅂ only before a vowel ending: 뵈었어요, but 뵙겠습니다.
Korean prefers the active voice for your own actions; -에 의해 is translationese.

mistakes.wrong: 그 일은 제가 하겠습니다. 그래서 팀장님과 상의하지 않았습니다.
mistakes.right: 그 일은 제가 하겠지만, 팀장님과 상의해야 합니다.
mistakes.why: 하겠지만 balances the promise against the requirement in one sentence.

task.title: Take two sides of one question
task.instructions: Choose a question you actually disagree with somebody about. Write the strongest version of the other side in three sentences, then your own in three, linking them with -지만, 반면에 and 따라서. Finish with the condition under which you would change your position.
